archetype.name: Bubble Team (slipping)
archetype.definition: A club coming off two near-playoff seasons whose 5-on-5 play has slid to below average, and whose special teams are now dragging it toward the bottom of the Metropolitan.

report.headline: Broken special teams are dragging a middling 5-on-5 team toward the bottom
report.take:
Columbus arrives at the end of October at 4-5-0, seventh in the Metropolitan and 28th of 32 on the site's board. The record flatters the play a little. The Blue Jackets have been outscored 30-22. All five losses came in regulation, several of them lopsided: 3-7 to Florida, 2-6 to Toronto, 1-4 to Utah. Every win since the 6-3 opener against Buffalo has needed overtime and been decided by one goal, including a 1-0 over the Rangers and a 2-1 over Vegas. That is a team scraping points, not earning them, and the 82-game pace of 73 points is a long way from last year's 92.

The biggest driver is special teams, and it isn't close. The power play is converting 11.5% (29th) against a league average of 21.2%. The penalty kill is stopping 71% (24th) against a league norm of 78.3%. At 5-on-5 the picture is mediocre rather than disastrous: a 49% shot-attempt share (17th) and a 47.6% expected-goals share (21st), with 5-on-5 PDO sitting at a neutral 100.1. So the gap between 'slightly below average' and 'bottom five' is mostly being lost on the power play and the kill.

The finishing numbers hide a split. All-situations shooting is 8.7% (27th) against a league 11.3%, and the all-situations PDO of 97.4 ranks 30th. Some of that is bad luck that should lift. Zach Werenski has 28 shots and no goals while playing 29 minutes a night, and Conor Garland has no points in nine games. But the 5-on-5 xGF slide from last season's 52% to 47.6% is a real step back, not luck. The individual xGF shares show why: Adam Fantilli (43.6%) and Kent Johnson (42.8%) are getting buried territorially in big minutes, while only Charlie Coyle (55.7%) is clearly winning his shifts. The third pair is worse. Erik Gudbranson ranks 238th of 250 defensemen on the site and Carson Soucy 235th, with expected-goals shares of 39.2% and 37.1%.

Where it goes from here: shooting should drift back toward normal and the power play can't stay this bad, so the offense should improve from its 2.44 goals a game. The 5-on-5 erosion and a thin blueline below the top three are structural, though. Without a real special-teams turnaround this looks like a team in the high 70s to mid 80s in points, chasing the race rather than in it.

strengths.title: Coyle anchoring the center depth
strengths.body: Charlie Coyle leads the team with 8 points and is its one regular forward clearly winning the expected-goals battle at 55.7%. Cole Sillinger, on a lower line, is also above water at 50.6% and has chipped in 6 points. Coyle's play-driving looks like the sturdiest part of the forward group and should hold. It also means a lot of the even-strength load sits on one veteran.

strengths.title: Goaltending roughly league average
strengths.body: The goalies are saving slightly more than expected as a group: team GSAx is 1.3, 15th and a touch above the league mean. Cam Talbot (+1.4 GSAx, .891) has been the steadier of the pair, while Jet Greaves (-0.4, .883) has the lone shutout. Neither is stealing games, but the goaltending isn't the reason Columbus is losing. Last year's +7.8 GSAx suggests the position can be a modest plus.

strengths.title: Possession is close to even
strengths.body: At 5-on-5 Columbus holds 49% of shot attempts, 17th, and its shots on goal for and against are both within a shot of the league average. The puck isn't being taken away from them wholesale. The problem is converting that possession into quality and goals. That base makes a recovery plausible if the finishing and special teams normalize.

concerns.title: Special teams are a disaster
concerns.body: A 11.5% power play and a 71% penalty kill both sit far below league averages of 21.2% and 78.3%. Neither unit ranks better than 24th, and that alone explains much of the negative goal differential. Over nine games both numbers carry a lot of noise and the power play should climb. Last year's units were only middling, though, so a full rebound to average isn't guaranteed.

concerns.title: Bottom pair getting caved in
concerns.body: Gudbranson and Soucy rank 238th and 235th of 250 defensemen on the site, with expected-goals shares of 39.2% and 37.1% and plus-minus marks of -7 and -5. That is why Werenski is logging 29 minutes a night. This looks structural rather than random, and it will keep leaking goals until the deployment changes.

concerns.title: 5-on-5 quality has slipped
concerns.body: The expected-goals share has fallen from 52% last season to 47.6%. Top-line centers Fantilli and Johnson are both under 44% individually. Wingers also produce an outsized share of the points scored against Columbus (43.4% against a league 38.8%). Unlike the shooting percentage, this is a play-driving decline that luck won't fix.

trend.note: The last five games produced a 2-3-0 record and just 1.8 goals a game, down from the season's 2.44. The two wins in that stretch needed overtime to finish 1-0 and 2-1.

weekAhead.headline: Three road games, two against top-four teams, then Colorado
weekAhead.body:
The week opens at Philadelphia, the one soft spot. The Flyers are 29th on the site, last in scoring and hold just 37.4% of 5-on-5 expected goals. Columbus should control that game territorially. The catch is the Flyers' goaltending: a .902 save percentage and +6.2 GSAx, fifth in the league, which is the worst possible matchup for a team shooting 8.7%. Then it gets hard. Carolina leads the league in shots per game (33.9) and holds 60% of expected goals. Dallas allows the fewest shots, ranks first in goals against and first in save percentage, and holds every position group furthest under its expected points. A bad power play meeting Dallas's 92.3% penalty kill is not a recipe for goals.

The home game against Colorado on November 3 is the most interesting. The Avalanche score at the second-highest rate in the league, but on a 105.4 PDO and 14% shooting that look unsustainable. Their goalies are at -5 GSAx (28th) and their penalty kill is 75%. If the Columbus power play is going to wake up, that is the night. Two points from Philadelphia and a split of the other three would be a decent week; anything more would be a surprise.

keyMatchups.title: Cold shooters against Flyers' goaltending
keyMatchups.body: Philadelphia gives up 31.4 shots a game but stops .902 of them, and Columbus is converting well below the league rate. This is the game the Blue Jackets should win on play. Whether they do comes down to beating a goalie tandem that has been one of the league's best at saving above expected.

keyMatchups.title: Surviving Carolina's shot volume
keyMatchups.body: Carolina leads the league at 33.9 shots a game and allows almost nothing to defensemen (2nd). Columbus's bottom pair will be exposed. The one opening is that centers produce well against the Hurricanes (24th), which suits a forward group led by Coyle, Fantilli and Johnson.

keyMatchups.title: Power play's best chance: Colorado
keyMatchups.body: Colorado's penalty kill (75%, 22nd) and goaltending (-5 GSAx) are both weak. It also ranks 28th at holding down both centers and defensemen. That opens a door for Werenski, who has 28 shots and no goals, and for the center-heavy top six.

weekAhead.watch: Whether the power play scores at all against Philadelphia and Colorado. Dallas's 92.3% kill won't offer much in between.

restOfSeason.body:
Some of this will correct. All-situations shooting well below the league average, Werenski without a goal and Garland without a point are the kind of slumps that ease over 73 games. The power play is unlikely to stay at 11.5%. I'd expect the offense to climb toward 2.6 to 2.9 goals a game and the power play into the 15-19% range. What won't fix itself is the 5-on-5 slide from last year's 52% xGF share and a bottom defense pair that is among the worst in the league by the site's rankings. Overtime wins built the current record; that is luck in close games, and it gives back as often as it gives.

The result is a team better than its 73-point pace but well short of last year's 92. I'd project 74 to 86 points and 33 to 39 wins, outside the playoff line unless the special teams flip completely. The ceiling is a return to last season's level if Fantilli and Johnson start winning their minutes. The floor is a bottom-five finish if the blueline depth keeps bleeding goals.
swingFactors: Power play climbing back toward league average
Fantilli and Johnson winning their 5-on-5 matchups

confidence.note: Nine games; special-teams and shooting rates are very noisy at this sample.
